newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Gold market seen ignoring Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Gold market seen ignoring Deng's death.

text.p: Gold prices are expected to show little reaction in Asia to news of the death of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, bullion dealers said on Thursday.
In early trading in Sydney, gold was fetching about US$346 an ounce, little changed from U.S. price levels.
"We're not expecting it to have a big effect on the market," said Mark Freemantle, senior bullion dealer for Rothschild Australia Ltd. "In fact, it's had no affect at all so far."
Market participants noted Deng had retired from politics in 1993 and that his successor, Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin, had been carefully groomed for the top leadership role.
Still, expectations of a rally in gold in the wake of the Chinese events underscored the precious metals diminishing role as a traditional "safe-haven" investment, dealers said.
"I don't think you're going to see people diving out of their portfolios and into gold," one bullion dealer said.
The Perth Mint quoted gold at US$345.53 and A$449.27 an ounce in early trading on Thursday.

"People always get nervous in times of change, but the death of Deng really comes as no surprise," said Simon Middleton, gold analyst for the Australian Bureau of Agricutultural and Resource Economics, the Australian government's commodity forecaster.

"China's political situation has been relatively stable for some time ... there's not that uncertainty over the future," Middleton said. He said gold was increasingly being viewed as a commodity, more influenced by supply and demand pressures.
"While some people will certainly hold gold because, if need be, they can carry it out in a suitcase, it's becoming more of a commodity," Middleton said.
Gold, which has risen for six consecutive days, albeit incrementally, is more likely to react to bullish sentiment surrounding the silver market, dealers said.
Silver reached a six-month high last week, partially owing to some gold bugs switching their preference for metals, one dealer said.

In the United States, the spot gold/silver ratio edged back up to 66.73 Wednesday, as gold began to catch up with silver's recovery, after the ratio saw a 22-month low last week. COMEX March silver ended down 3.0 cents at US$5.185 an ounce.
"Those crossovers are now largely over and gold can ride more comnfortably on the tail of a firm silver market," the dealer said.

In local trading, gold mining companies have been active on both sides of the market in recent days, with further buying anticipated if gold shows a willingness to breach $US$350 an ounce, dealers said.
"If it goes to $350 we'll also see more of the speculative players," one said.
Brisk demand for physical metal from jewellery makers and other fabricators was still evident, although as prices creep upward, that consumption is expected to taper, dealers said.
